The client told me three times the wall was straight. The client was standing in front of the wall. The client could not see the wall.

The wall is a 1920s extension, built by a man who was very keen on doing things his own way.

Customer looks at the wall. Fitter looks at the reveal. Surveyor looks at the reveal. Office looks at the spreadsheet. Everyone agrees the reveal is fine.

Meanwhile the lintel is 12mm out of level, the cavity is full of 1980s expanding foam, and there is a cast iron soil pipe sitting exactly where the frame needs to go.

The window was never the problem.

posts.hook: Things a fitter knows that a customer never will

caption.ig:
Things a fitter knows that a customer never will

Things a fitter knows that the customer never will:

1. That cill needs a 5mm fall and it will never have one
2. The trickle vent is 40mm from the head and the head is 40mm lower than the drawing
3. That wall is 8mm out of plumb and will stay that way forever
4. The old frame was packed with a rolled-up newspaper from 1994
5. The colour will look different in this light and there is nothing anyone can do about it

Nobody asked. Nobody ever asks. We just know.

posts.hook: My least favourite four words in the English language.

caption.ig:
My least favourite four words in the English language.

“Is it meant to do that?”

You are 40 minutes into a fitting. The room is upside down. There is foam on the floor and a vacuum cleaner that stopped working in 2011.

“Will it stop doing that when the glass is in?”

No. It will stop doing that when I shim the bottom corner. Give me nine minutes.

“You’ve got nine minutes?”

I do not.

posts.hook: There is a difference between “scribed” and “fudged”

caption.ig:
There is a difference between “scribed” and “fudged”

Scribing is cutting the horn at an angle to follow the wall.

Fudging is cutting the horn at an angle and hoping the wall is what you thought it was.

They look identical from the outside. From the inside one is a joint line and one is a 6mm gap with a bead of silicone holding the world together.

The customer will find the difference. In eight years. On a Tuesday. Quietly.

Everybody in the trade knows somebody who calls it the wrong one and will not be corrected.

An astragal is the glazing bar itself — the timber or profile sitting between the panes.

An astragal bar is the metal or plastic insert that clips into it.

You can tell the difference by whether it makes a noise in the wind. If it does, you’ve got a bar and a gap.

posts.hook: Cill projection: the number nobody ever agrees on

caption.ig:
Cill projection: the number nobody ever agrees on

65mm is standard.
75mm is better in the rain.
85mm is what your dad’s has got.

Then you get to the brickwork, and the brickwork has been repointed twice since 1974 and the face is now 12mm further out than the drawing, so your 65mm cill is now a 53mm cill, and now it is not standard and not better in the rain, it is just wet.

Standardise your cill projection. Write it on the job. Then argue about it once, in writing, forever.

posts.hook: A bay is not a bay. It is a geometry.

caption.ig:
A bay is not a bay. It is a geometry.

A 45° canted bay loses about 30% of its glass to sightlines.

A 30° bay loses about 17%.

A 90° box gives you a structural pier in the middle of your living room wall.

Add a return on the end, add a door under it, add a monkey bar on top, and suddenly your “45 degree bay” is a bespoke fabrication with its own drawing, its own price and its own eight-week lead time.

It was always going to be bespoke. It was always going to have a drawing. Have the drawing before the customer picks the tile.

posts.hook: Turn a corner: casement, tilt & turn, french, or all three?

caption.ig:
Turn a corner: casement, tilt & turn, french, or all three?

Casement: cheapest, opens out, hinges eat clear glass.

Tilt & turn: opens in for cleaning, hinges invisible, hardware costs more.

French: two sashes, no mullion, doubles the sightline risk, best with a shallow reveal.

All three: a bifold, and now the lead time is six weeks and the hinge selection is the whole project.

Get this wrong on a ground floor rear elevation and someone is leaning out of a first floor window to clean it for the next fifteen years.

posts.hook: The 30-second window nerd test

caption.ig:
The 30-second window nerd test

Ask a window fitter these and watch their eyes light up:

1. What’s your cill projection?
2. Sash weight or rope and pulley?
3. What grade of stainless for the coastal job?

posts.hook: Five things that turn a good install into a bad one

caption.ig:
Five things that turn a good install into a bad one

1. The foam. Too little and it moves, too much and it bows the frame.
2. The fixings. Into the reveal, into solid, never into the old frame.
3. The gaps. If the perimeter gap is not consistent, the sealant tells the truth eventually.
4. The sill. Level, with fall, horned, and cut to the wall not to the paper.
5. The protection. If it isn’t taped, it will be marked. If it isn’t boarded, it will be scratched.

Five things. That is the craft.

posts.hook: What Article 4 actually does (in a way nobody explains it)

caption.ig:
What Article 4 actually does (in a way nobody explains it)

Slide 1: Normally, in England, replacing windows in a house is permitted development. No permission. Just do it.

Slide 2: Article 4 takes that right away from you in a specific direction — usually the front — usually to protect a view.

Slide 3: In a conservation area the same applies, and in Scotland since May 2024, prior notification applies to a lot of listed and street-facing windows.

Slide 4: On a listed building you need listed building consent and uPVC is basically never acceptable.

Slide 5: The mistake: finding out all of this after you have surveyed, specified and quoted.

Conservation area, Article 4 and listed status, flagged before you knock. fenora.pro

posts.hook: Myth: bigger glass means a better window

caption.ig:
Myth: bigger glass means a better window

Slide 1: “You can have more glass.” Yes. You can also have a weaker frame, a bigger sightline problem and a heavier unit.

Slide 2: Glass area is set by the frame, the bar and the structural requirement — not by ambition.

Slide 3: A 2,180mm frame in a 1,900mm opening is not slim sightlines. It is a structural claim.

Slide 4: The right question is not “how much glass”. It is “how much glass, in what frame, at what sightline, at what weight”.

Slide 5: That is a specification conversation. Not a brochure.

posts.hook: Myth: all double glazing is the same glass

caption.ig:
Myth: all double glazing is the same glass

Slide 1: There is a 2mm difference in cavity width, which is a 12% difference in energy loss.

Slide 2: There is argon and there is air, and it is about 15% of the U-value.

Slide 3: There is warm edge and there is aluminium, and it matters at the perimeter, which is where the loss actually is.

Slide 4: There is a coated face and there is a clear face, and it has to go the right way up or it is worse than nothing.

Slide 5: There is no such thing as a standard sealed unit. Ask for the make-up in millimetres and watch what happens.

posts.hook: The window industry has a data problem, not a sales problem

caption.ig:
The window industry has a data problem, not a sales problem

Nobody in UK window manufacturing is short of work.

What they are short of is certainty. Certainty about what was quoted. What was surveyed. What was ordered. What was made. What was delivered. What was paid.

Six organisations, six systems, and one person — usually the most overloaded person in the company — responsible for the integrity of the whole chain.

The remake rate in this industry is a direct, measurable function of how many systems a job passes through. It is not a quality problem. Quality is the best part of this trade. It is a reconciliation problem.

The fix is not better salespeople or better ads. It is one record that carries the specification, the price, the evidence and the history from enquiry to final invoice, written once and read everywhere.

It is not glamorous. It is the whole thing.

posts.hook: We built a job finder because nobody else bothered

caption.ig:
We built a job finder because nobody else bothered

There is a public register of every planning application in the United Kingdom. It is free. It is searchable. It contains, in plain English, what people are applying to build on specific addresses.

Roughly one in six of those applications includes window or door work worth quoting.

Almost nobody is using it. The reason is not a lack of access — it is that turning a PDF into a lead, and a lead into a survey, and a survey into a quote requires a person with a highlighter and a lot of free time.

We built it into the platform instead. Search by radius, by application type, by date. Flag conservation area, Article 4 and listed status. Estimate units and likely specification. Add it to the pipeline as a real record with the address and the works attached.

The interesting part is not the search. It is that the job arrives in the system already connected to surveying, configuring, quoting and delivery, so nobody has to rebuild it in six other tools.

If you install windows, this is a free, permanent, uncrowded pipeline in your own area. It has been sitting there the entire time.

posts.hook: Why we will not publish a customer testimonial

caption.ig:
Why we will not publish a customer testimonial

We could have a wall of them tomorrow. That was available to us on day one.

The reason we have not is that every customer we have is a window business, and a window business that publishes its own margin, its own remake rate and its own quoting failures to a software vendor's website has taken a risk it did not need to take.

So we will not ask.

What we will publish instead is four measures: time to quote, remakes, margin held against margin quoted, and re-entries per job. Real businesses, real figures, agreed in writing before anything goes on the site.

We have none of those published yet. Not because we do not track them, but because we do not have permission from the right number of people.

That is a slower way to build trust. It is also the only way that survives a reference call.

The four measures we hold ourselves to. fenora.pro

posts.hook: Window businesses do not lose money in the factory

caption.ig:
Window businesses do not lose money in the factory

They lose it in four places that almost nobody writes down.

One: the survey. An opening comes in 9mm out, it becomes a wedge, a second visit and a morning, and it is absorbed because the quote was a lump sum with a fitting percentage buried inside it.

Two: the office. The specification is re-keyed between systems, and once it is re-keyed it belongs to whoever keyed it last.

Three: the second visit. “Just while you're here” has no scope, no price and no owner, and it is the single most expensive sentence in domestic construction.

Four: delivery. A 2,180mm frame on an unsuitable vehicle becomes two vans, and two vans are rarely in anybody's model.

None of this is a manufacturing problem. The manufacturing in this industry is genuinely world class.

It is a data problem, and data problems are cheap to fix and expensive to ignore.

Price the fitting. Carry the variation. fenora.pro

Four: delivery. A 2,180mm frame on an unsuitable vehicle becomes two vans, and two vans are rarely in anybody's model.

None of this is a manufacturing problem. The manufacturing in this industry is genuinely world class.

It is a data problem, and data problems are cheap to fix and expensive to ignore.

Price the fitting. Carry the variation. fenora.pro

posts.hook: The spreadsheet is not a cheap version of quoting software

caption.ig:
The spreadsheet is not a cheap version of quoting software

It is a shared, mutable document with no version history, no permissions, no validation and no relationship to anything else in the business.

Every modification overwrites the last. Two people cannot work in it at once. Nothing enforces that a width is a number. Nothing knows that opening W0.2 belongs to a survey that belongs to a job that belongs to a customer.

And the cell that somebody changed last Thursday — the one that moves a casement from 1200 to 1186 — has no record of who changed it, when, or why, and by the time anybody notices, the frame is on a van.

A spreadsheet is a genuinely useful tool. It is a terrible system of record.

The distinction matters because most small businesses have quietly decided that the spreadsheet is the system. It is not the system. It is the place the data goes to get lost.

No spreadsheets. One record. fenora.pro
